exhibits.title: The Rank Dial
exhibits.text:
A brass instrument set on a plinth: a graduated DIAL clicking through the settings 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 — the rank r — and beside it a glowing RUNE you may turn independently, the strength alpha. Magister Quillon keeps them side by side to teach that they are TWO separate choices, forever confused by novices.

The dial sets HOW MANY directions the adapter is allowed — the width r of the narrow waist in B*A, the size of the subspace in which the update may live. Turn it too low and the adapter cannot capture the change the task demands: it UNDERFITS. Turn it too high and you pay in parameters and compute, invite OVERFITTING on small data, and eventually gain nothing over training every weight. There is no formula stamped on the dial. You find its setting by TURNING it — a sweep — and watching where the validation regret stops improving.

The rune sets HOW STRONGLY the adapter speaks, its magnitude — decoupled from how many directions it uses. This is the same knob you have already met: the strength slider on a ComfyUI LoRA. Study the two plinths to learn each in turn: first the dial and the underfit/overfit trade, then the rune and the alpha/r scaling that gives it its precise meaning.

exhibits.title: Choosing the Rank r
exhibits.text:
r is a HYPERPARAMETER — a number you choose, not one the training computes for you. There is no closed-form rule; there is a trade-off with two cliffs:

  - r TOO SMALL: the adapter's subspace is narrower than the update the task needs. It cannot represent the change — it UNDERFITS, and validation regret stays stubbornly high.
  - r TOO LARGE: more parameters and compute for no gain; on limited data the extra capacity OVERFITS; and past a point you are no better off than full fine-tuning, having thrown away LoRA's whole advantage.

Typical settings, by how far the model must move:
  - r = 4, 8, 16 — the workhorse range for most LLM and diffusion tuning (a style, a voice, a domain the base already half-knows).
  - r = 32, 64 — harder tasks or larger domain shifts.
  - r = 128, 256 — rare; near-relearning, where low rank buys little.

What guides the choice: how fast the update's singular values decay (its EFFECTIVE RANK — a steep spectrum wants a small r, a flat one a larger r), how far the new task sits from the base, how much data you have, and how many weight matrices you are adapting. The practical rule: SWEEP r and pick the SMALLEST value at which the validation curve PLATEAUS. That plateau is you having covered the effective rank — every direction beyond it is spent on noise.

exhibits.title: The Strength Rune — Alpha
exhibits.text:
The adapter is not simply added to the frozen weight. It is added through a SCALING:

  W_new = W + (alpha / r) * B * A

The factor alpha/r sets the MAGNITUDE of the adapter's contribution — how loudly the low-rank branch speaks — and, crucially, DECOUPLES that magnitude from the rank r. Divide by r and you can change how many directions the adapter uses WITHOUT its overall strength lurching; alpha then tunes the loudness on its own axis. Common conventions set alpha = r (so the scale is 1) or alpha = 2r (so the branch speaks at double weight); either way, raising r no longer silently amplifies the update.

This alpha is not a new creature. It is EXACTLY the strength slider you drag on a LoRA node in ComfyUI: that slider scales the (alpha/r)*B*A branch's contribution to the frozen model. Push it toward zero and the adapter fades and the base model returns; push it up and the adaptation dominates — sometimes past the point of coherence. Rank chooses how many directions; alpha chooses how hard to lean on them. Two dials, two questions, never the same one.

exhibits.title: Sweeping r to the Plateau
exhibits.spec:
graph LR
  R8["train r=8"] --> V8["val regret: high"]
  R16["train r=16"] --> V16["val regret: lower"]
  R32["train r=32"] --> V32["val regret: ~same as 16"]
  V8 --> D{"still improving?"}
  V16 --> D
  V32 --> D
  D -->|"plateau at r=16"| PICK["pick smallest r at plateau: r=16"]
exhibits.caption: Train at r = 8, 16, 32 and read the validation regret. From 8 to 16 it drops sharply (r=8 was underfitting); from 16 to 32 it barely moves — the curve has PLATEAUED. Pick the smallest r on the plateau (here 16): you have covered the update's effective rank, and larger r only adds parameters, compute, and overfitting risk for no gain.

exhibits.title: The Plateau Found
exhibits.caption: The two dials of the instrument, read as curves. LEFT — turning the rank dial: train at r = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and watch the validation. It climbs steeply while r is too small (the shaded UNDERFIT country, where the adapter's subspace is narrower than the update the task needs), then flattens into a PLATEAU. The rule of the hall: take the SMALLEST r on that plateau — here r is about 16 — for you have just covered the update's effective rank, and every direction past it is spent on noise. Turn further into the shaded DIMINISHING-RETURNS country and you pay in parameters, compute, and overfitting risk for no gain. RIGHT — turning the strength rune apart from it: the plotted quantity is the (alpha/r) factor that multiplies B*A in W_new = W + (alpha/r)*B*A. Hold the convention alpha = r and that factor stays pinned at 1 however far you turn the rank dial; hold alpha = 2r and it sits steady at 2, merely louder. But leave alpha FIXED and untie it from r, and the factor lurches — from 8 down toward a whisper — so raising r would quietly change the update's strength. Dividing by r is precisely what decouples loudness from rank. This alpha is the same knob as ComfyUI's strength slider. The values are representative — the SHAPE is the lesson.
